learn: Energy is the ability to cause change or do work.
Moving objects have kinetic energy. Stored energy is potential energy, like a stretched rubber band or a ball at the top of a hill.
Energy can change from one form to another but is never created or destroyed.
lessons.try: Roll a ball down ramps of different heights and observe how far it goes.

learn: The faster an object moves, the more kinetic energy it has.
A ball rolled from higher up gains more speed and energy.
A faster bowling ball knocks down more pins because it has more energy.
check: A ball from higher up gains...
lessons.try: Drop a ball from 30 cm and 90 cm onto sand. Compare the craters.

learn: When objects collide, energy transfers between them.
Some energy changes into sound and heat during a collision.
Engineers design bumpers and helmets to absorb collision energy.
lessons.try: Roll one marble into another and observe what happens.

units.t: Energy Transfer: Heat, Light, Sound and Electricity

learn: Heat energy moves from warmer objects to cooler ones.
Conductors, like metal, let heat move easily. Insulators, like wood, plastic and wool, slow heat flow.
A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot; a wooden spoon stays cooler.
check: Which is a good heat conductor?
lessons.try: Place metal, plastic and wooden spoons in warm water. Which handle warms fastest?

learn: Electricity is the flow of electric charge.
A circuit is a complete path for electricity: a battery, wires and a device like a bulb.
In an open circuit, the path is broken and the bulb goes out. A switch opens and closes a circuit.
check: What happens in an open circuit?
lessons.try: Draw a simple circuit with a battery, wires, a switch and a bulb.

learn: Electrical conductors include copper and other metals. Insulators include rubber and plastic.
Wires are copper covered in plastic so electricity flows inside but not to your hand.
Never touch outlets, play near power lines or use electrical devices near water.
check: Should you use electrical devices near water?
lessons.try: Make a home safety checklist for electricity.

learn: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another.
Waves have crests (high points) and troughs (low points).
Amplitude is the height of a wave. Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next.
check: The high point of a wave is the...
The distance from crest to crest is the...
lessons.try: Shake a rope or slinky to make waves. Change your speed and watch.

learn: Water waves move energy across the surface, but the water itself mostly moves up and down.
Sound travels as waves of vibration through air, water and solids.
Larger amplitude sound waves are louder.
check: In a water wave, the water mostly moves...
lessons.try: Float a cork in a tub and make waves. Does the cork travel across or bob in place?

learn: Patterns of waves can carry information.
Morse code sends messages with long and short signals.
Radio, mobile phones and Wi-Fi send information using invisible waves.
lessons.try: Send a Morse code message to a family member with a flashlight.

learn: Light travels in straight lines from a source.
When light hits an object, it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted (pass through).
We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes.
check: Reflects off them into our eyes
lessons.try: Use a flashlight and mirrors to bounce light around a corner.

learn: Light enters the eye through the pupil, the black opening.
The lens focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye.
The retina sends signals to the brain through the optic nerve.
check: Light enters the eye through the...
Signals go to the brain through the...
lessons.try: In a mirror, watch your pupils change size when you turn on a light.

learn: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one material to another, like air to water.
A straw in water looks bent because of refraction.
A prism splits white light into a rainbow of colours.
check: A prism splits white light into...
lessons.try: Put a pencil in a glass of water and look from the side.

learn: Living things have structures that help them survive, grow and reproduce.
External structures are outside, like a bird's feathers or a plant's thorns.
Internal structures are inside, like an animal's heart or a plant's xylem tubes that carry water.
lessons.try: List three internal and three external structures of a human.

learn: Roots absorb water and anchor the plant. Stems support and transport.
Leaves capture sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.
Flowers attract pollinators and make seeds; thorns protect from animals.
check: What protects some plants from animals?
lessons.try: Dissect a flower with a grown-up and identify its parts.

learn: Animals have structures for eating, moving, protection and senses.
Owls have large eyes for night vision. Snakes have flexible jaws to swallow large prey.
Many animals have skeletons for support: inside (endoskeleton) or outside (exoskeleton, like insects).
check: Why do owls have large eyes?
lessons.try: Compare the structures of a fish and a bird.

learn: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch collect information from the environment.
Each sense organ has receptors: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.
Receptors turn information into signals sent along nerves.
check: How many basic senses do we list?
lessons.try: Do a blindfolded taste test with a grown-up to explore smell and taste.

learn: The brain receives signals, processes them and decides how to respond.
Nerves carry messages between the brain and body.
Some responses are reflexes that happen automatically, like pulling your hand away from something hot.
lessons.try: Test your reaction time by catching a dropped ruler.

learn: Animals use senses in amazing ways.
Bats and dolphins use echolocation: they make sounds and listen to echoes.
Sharks sense electricity from prey. Dogs have a sense of smell many times stronger than ours.
check: Dogs have a very strong sense of...
lessons.try: Research one animal with a special sense.

learn: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces.
Physical weathering includes ice wedging: water freezes in cracks, expands and splits rock.
Chemical weathering happens when water and air change the minerals in rock, like rust.
lessons.try: Shake rough rocks in a jar of water and watch them become smoother over days.

learn: Erosion moves weathered rock and soil to new places.
Water, wind, ice (glaciers) and gravity cause erosion.
Deposition is when the material is dropped in a new place, like a river delta.
check: Dropping material in a new place is...
lessons.try: Build a sand hill and pour water on it. Where does the sand go?

learn: The Grand Canyon was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years.
Glaciers carved U-shaped valleys. Wind shapes sand dunes and arches.
Plant roots can slow erosion by holding soil.
lessons.try: Compare pictures of a V-shaped river valley and a U-shaped glacier valley.

learn: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment, like sand and mud, are pressed together over time.
Usually, the bottom layers are oldest and the top layers are youngest.
Scientists read rock layers like pages in a history book.
check: In rock layers, the oldest are usually at the...
lessons.try: Make layers of different coloured sand in a jar.

learn: Fossils in a layer show what lived when that layer formed.
Marine fossils in a desert show the area was once underwater.
Index fossils help scientists match layers in different places.
check: Marine fossils in a desert show...
lessons.try: Look at a diagram of rock layers with fossils and describe the area's history.

learn: Rock layers can be bent, tilted or broken by forces in Earth.
Canyons expose many layers, like the Grand Canyon, which shows nearly 2 billion years of history.
Scientists use evidence to explain how landscapes changed.
check: Rock layers can be bent by...
lessons.try: Fold layers of clay to model how rock layers bend.

learn: Maps show patterns: mountains, ocean trenches, volcanoes and earthquake zones.
Many volcanoes and earthquakes happen along the edges of tectonic plates.
The "Ring of Fire" around the Pacific Ocean has many volcanoes.
check: In the middle of every plate
The Ring of Fire surrounds the...
lessons.try: Look at a map of volcanoes and earthquakes. What pattern do you notice?

learn: Earthquakes happen when plates suddenly move along faults.
Seismographs measure earthquake strength.
During an earthquake: drop, cover and hold on.
lessons.try: Practise drop, cover and hold on at home.

learn: Volcanoes form where magma rises through Earth's crust.
Lava is magma that reaches the surface. Eruptions can release ash and gases.
Volcanic islands like Hawaii formed from eruptions under the ocean.
check: Magma that reaches the surface is...
lessons.try: Draw and label a cross-section of a volcano.

learn: Natural resources come from Earth: water, soil, minerals, plants and fuels.
Renewable energy sources, like sunlight, wind and moving water, are replaced naturally.
Nonrenewable sources, like coal, oil and natural gas, took millions of years to form and can run out.
check: Coal, oil and natural gas are...
lessons.try: List energy sources used in your home and classify them.

learn: Burning fossil fuels can pollute air and water.
Mining and drilling can damage habitats.
Renewable sources usually cause less pollution but have their own trade-offs, like land use.
lessons.try: Compare the pros and cons of solar and coal power in a table.

learn: Conservation means using resources wisely so they last.
Reduce, reuse and recycle. Turn off lights. Use less water.
Engineers design solutions like solar panels, wind turbines and efficient cars.
lessons.try: Make a plan for your family to save energy this week.
